extracted.intended_audience: general literate readers of The Spectator; students/scholars of 18th-century essays and satire
extracted.subtask_description: Short, moralizing humorous essays in the vein of The Spectator: epistolary pieces, satirical commentary, fables and anecdotes that instruct while entertaining. Emphasizes naturalness, illustrative anecdotes, and allegory to teach prudence and social criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for touches of nature over wit
rubrics_metrics.description: I am more pleased with a Letter that is filled with Touches of Nature than of Wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuate correspondence and short pieces for natural, humane detail rather than mere cleverness. Pieces that move by simple, believable feeling (e.g., domestic letters about family estrangement) are preferred; avoid artificial cleverness that lacks sympathy or 'touches of nature.' Examples in the text: a wife's pleading letter about parental estrangement is held up as superior to witty but less moving writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fables should convey instruction without offending authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Fables... had so good an Effect, as to convey Instruction to the Ear of a King without offending it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fables as a vehicle for moral or political instruction where direct address would offend or be rejected. Choose allegory to present critique gently — appropriate when addressing powerful or sensitive audiences; employ indirect examples to effect persuasion rather than blunt reproach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of fables: beasts/vegetables vs. personified passions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fables I have here mentioned are raised altogether upon Brutes and Vegetables... but besides this kind of Fable, there is another in which the Actors are Passions, Virtues, Vices, and other imaginary Persons of the like Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing a fable, select the form that best fits the moral aim: animal/vegetable fables for external, easily pictured lessons; allegorical fables (personified passions/virtues) for psychological or philosophical points. Mix humans among beasts/vegetables only when the moral requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use personification to map traits to characters
rubrics_metrics.description: the several Names of Gods and Heroes are nothing else but the Affections of the Mind in a visible Shape and Character. Thus they tell us, that Achilles...represents Anger, or the Irascible Part of Human Nature; That...Pallas is only another Name for Reason...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ concrete characters to embody abstract qualities (e.g., Anger, Reason) so readers can perceive internal conflicts externally. Explicit mapping (as in classical exempla) helps readers grasp moral/psychological points; give sensory or behavioural traits that signal the abstraction embodied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fables to gain attention of stubborn or inflamed audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: we see a Mutiny among the Common People appeased by a Fable of the Belly and the Limbs, which was indeed very proper to gain the Attention of an incensed Rabble, at a Time when perhaps they would have torn to Pieces any Man who had preached the same Doctrine to them in an open and direct Manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To reach hostile or inflamed crowds, prefer illustrative fables over direct preaching. A well-chosen allegory can defuse anger and lead to reflection where direct moralizing would be rejected or inflame passions further.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fables flourish with learned, cultivated audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: As Fables took their Birth in the very Infancy of Learning, they never flourished more than when Learning was at its greatest Height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match fable complexity and classical allusion to the audience's learning: highly learned audiences appreciate layered allegory and classical references (Horace, Boileau, La Fontaine), while simpler fables suit less erudite readerships. Consider audience sophistication when choosing density of allusion and moral subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate conquests by concrete costs and gains (subjects, riches, power)
rubrics_metrics.description: As for himself, it is certain he can have gained nothing by his Conquests, if they have not rendered him Master of more Subjects, more Riches, or greater Power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging political/military ambition, weigh measurable benefits (increase in subjects, wealth, power) against tangible costs: military casualties, famine, depopulation, economic dislocation, and demographic/psychological effects (reduced marriage, industry). Use quantification and historical examples (e.g., Flemish population counts, estimated army losses, Pyrrhus anecdote) to argue that apparent victories may be net losses (Pyrrhic victories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anecdotes and historical exempla to illustrate moral points
rubrics_metrics.description: When he had shewn the utmost Fondness for his Expedition against the Romans, Cyneas his chief Minister asked him what he proposed to himself by this War?... (Pyrrhus story) ... Eginhart...story recorded in an old Chronicle...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End or bolster essays with concise historical or legendary anecdotes (classical or medieval) to dramatize and concretize abstract moral claims. Well-chosen exempla (Pyrrhus, Eginhart) provide memorable closure and authoritative precedent; prefer stories that mirror the essay's central lesson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical/social-critique aim: make moral crimes socially infamous
rubrics_metrics.description: It is in the Power of you, and such as I hope you are, to make it as infamous to rob a poor Creature of her Honour as her Cloaths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming social critique at specific abuses (e.g., seduction/insnaring of women), write to shift public stigma and legal attention: equate moral wrongs with recognized crimes to mobilize public opinion and authorities. Tactics include publishing vivid first-person letters, prosecutorial narratives, and public condemnation to change norms and enforcement practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to natural sympathy and reciprocal moral principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all Hardnesses of Heart there is none so inexcusable as that of Parents towards their Children... We make it the Condition of our Forgiveness that we forgive others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In moral essays, ground arguments in natural sympathy and reciprocal ethical maxims (e.g., forgiveness begets forgiveness). Use theological and prudential reasoning together to persuade: appeal both to instinctive human compassion and to the inconsistency of demanding divine forgiveness while refusing human forgiveness.
